title: 02. Data Structures: Python Dictionaries - Complete Mastery Guide
summary: A dictionary is a mutable, unordered collection of key-value pairs. Keys must be unique and immutable (strings, numbers, tuples).

sections.title: 1. Introduction to Dictionaries {#introduction}
sections.body:
A dictionary is a mutable, unordered collection of key-value pairs. Keys must be unique and immutable (strings, numbers, tuples).

### Basic Syntax

```python
# Creating dictionaries
empty_dict = {}
dict_literal = {'name': 'John', 'age': 30, 'city': 'New York'}
dict_constructor = dict(name='John', age=30, city='New York')
dict_from_pairs = dict([('name', 'John'), ('age', 30)])

# Using zip to create dictionaries
keys = ['name', 'age', 'city']
values = ['John', 30, 'New York']
zipped_dict = dict(zip(keys, values))
```

diagrams.title: How a dict finds a key
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  k["d['email']"] --> h["hash('email')"] --> idx["index = hash & (table size − 1)"]
  idx --> slot{"slot state"}
  slot -->|empty| miss["KeyError / insert here"]
  slot -->|"same hash and key == 'email'"| hit["return value — O(1) on average"]
  slot -->|"different key — collision"| probe["probe the next slot"] --> slot
diagrams.explain: A dict is a hash table: the key's `hash()` picks a slot directly, so lookups do not scan. That is why keys must be **hashable** (immutable) and why two equal keys must have equal hashes. Since Python 3.7 dicts also preserve insertion order, thanks to the compact layout with a separate entries array.

sections.title: 2. Basic Dictionary Operations {#basic-operations}
sections.body:
### Accessing and Modifying

```python
person = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25, 'profession': 'Engineer'}

# Accessing values
print(person['name'])           # Direct access (KeyError if key doesn't exist)
print(person.get('name'))       # Safe access (returns None if key doesn't exist)
print(person.get('salary', 0))  # Default value if key doesn't exist

# Adding/Updating values
person['salary'] = 75000        # Add new key-value pair
person['age'] = 26             # Update existing value
person.update({'city': 'Boston', 'country': 'USA'})  # Update multiple

# Deleting items
del person['profession']        # Delete specific key
age = person.pop('age')        # Remove and return value
item = person.popitem()        # Remove and return arbitrary item (LIFO in Python 3.7+)
person.clear()                 # Remove all items
```

### Checking Membership

```python
data = {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3}

# Check if key exists
print('a' in data)              # True
print('d' not in data)         # True

# Check if value exists (less efficient)
print(1 in data.values())      # True
print(4 not in data.values())  # True
```

sections.title: 3. Dictionary Methods {#dictionary-methods}
sections.body:
### Essential Methods

```python
student = {'name': 'Bob', 'grade': 'A', 'subjects': ['Math', 'Science']}

# Getting keys, values, and items
keys_list = list(student.keys())        # ['name', 'grade', 'subjects']
values_list = list(student.values())    # ['Bob', 'A', ['Math', 'Science']]
items_list = list(student.items())      # [('name', 'Bob'), ('grade', 'A'), ...]

# Dictionary views (dynamic)
keys_view = student.keys()              # dict_keys object
values_view = student.values()          # dict_values object
items_view = student.items()            # dict_items object

# Copying dictionaries
shallow_copy = student.copy()           # Shallow copy
import copy
deep_copy = copy.deepcopy(student)      # Deep copy

# Setting default values
grades = {'Alice': 85, 'Bob': 90}
grades.setdefault('Charlie', 0)         # Adds Charlie: 0 if not exists
print(grades)                           # {'Alice': 85, 'Bob': 90, 'Charlie': 0}
```

### Advanced Methods with Examples

```python
# Using fromkeys() to create dictionaries
subjects = ['Math', 'Science', 'English']
grades = dict.fromkeys(subjects, 'Not Graded')
print(grades)  # {'Math': 'Not Graded', 'Science': 'Not Graded', 'English': 'Not Graded'}

# Multiple default values (careful with mutable defaults!)
# Wrong way:
wrong_scores = dict.fromkeys(['Alice', 'Bob'], [])  # Shares same list!

# Right way:
students = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie']
scores = {student: [] for student in students}      # Each gets own list
```

sections.body:
### Dictionaries with Lists

```python
# Dictionary of lists
course_students = {
    'Math': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],
    'Science': ['Alice', 'Diana', 'Eve'],
    'English': ['Bob', 'Charlie', 'Diana']
}

# Adding to lists in dictionary
course_students['Math'].append('Frank')
course_students.setdefault('History', []).append('Grace')

# List of dictionaries
employees = [
    {'name': 'Alice', 'department': 'Engineering', 'salary': 75000},
    {'name': 'Bob', 'department': 'Marketing', 'salary': 65000},
    {'name': 'Charlie', 'department': 'Engineering', 'salary': 80000}
]

# Operations on list of dictionaries
engineers = [emp for emp in employees if emp['department'] == 'Engineering']
total_salary = sum(emp['salary'] for emp in employees)
avg_engineering_salary = sum(emp['salary'] for emp in engineers) / len(engineers)
```

### Dictionaries with Tuples

```python
# Dictionary with tuple keys (coordinates)
board_game = {
    (0, 0): 'empty', (0, 1): 'player1', (0, 2): 'empty',
    (1, 0): 'player2', (1, 1): 'empty', (1, 2): 'player1',
    (2, 0): 'empty', (2, 1): 'player2', (2, 2): 'empty'
}

# Dictionary with tuple values
student_grades = {
    'Alice': ('A', 95, 'Excellent'),
    'Bob': ('B+', 87, 'Good'),
    'Charlie': ('A-', 92, 'Very Good')
}

# Named tuples with dictionaries
from collections import namedtuple

Grade = namedtuple('Grade', ['letter', 'score', 'comment'])
student_grades_named = {
    'Alice': Grade('A', 95, 'Excellent'),
    'Bob': Grade('B+', 87, 'Good'),
    'Charlie': Grade('A-', 92, 'Very Good')
}

print(student_grades_named['Alice'].score)  # 95
```

### Dictionaries with Sets

```python
# Dictionary with set values
student_subjects = {
    'Alice': {'Math', 'Science', 'English'},
    'Bob': {'Math', 'History', 'Art'},
    'Charlie': {'Science', 'English', 'History'}
}

# Finding common subjects between students
alice_bob_common = student_subjects['Alice'] & student_subjects['Bob']
all_subjects = set().union(*student_subjects.values())

# Dictionary for set operations
departments = {
    'tech': {'Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'},
    'marketing': {'Diana', 'Eve', 'Frank'},
    'sales': {'Bob', 'Grace', 'Henry'}  # Bob works in both tech and sales
}

# Find employees in multiple departments
tech_employees = departments['tech']
sales_employees = departments['sales']
cross_department = tech_employees & sales_employees
```

sections.title: 7. Lambda Functions with Dictionaries {#lambda-functions}
sections.body:
### Sorting Dictionaries with Lambda

```python
# Sort by keys
scores = {'Alice': 95, 'Charlie': 87, 'Bob': 92}
sorted_by_key = dict(sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: x[0]))
print(sorted_by_key)  # {'Alice': 95, 'Bob': 92, 'Charlie': 87}

# Sort by values
sorted_by_value = dict(sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True))
print(sorted_by_value)  # {'Alice': 95, 'Bob': 92, 'Charlie': 87}

# Complex sorting with lambda
employees = [
    {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30, 'salary': 70000},
    {'name': 'Bob', 'age': 25, 'salary': 65000},
    {'name': 'Charlie', 'age': 35, 'salary': 80000}
]

# Sort by salary descending, then by age ascending
sorted_employees = sorted(employees, key=lambda x: (-x['salary'], x['age']))
```

### Filtering with Lambda

```python
# Filter dictionary items
products = {
    'laptop': 999.99,
    'mouse': 25.50,
    'keyboard': 75.00,
    'monitor': 299.99,
    'headphones': 150.00
}

# Filter expensive items
expensive_items = dict(filter(lambda item: item[1] > 100, products.items()))
print(expensive_items)  # {'laptop': 999.99, 'monitor': 299.99, 'headphones': 150.00}

# Filter with complex conditions
students = {
    'Alice': {'grade': 95, 'attendance': 0.95},
    'Bob': {'grade': 75, 'attendance': 0.80},
    'Charlie': {'grade': 88, 'attendance': 0.92}
}

honor_students = dict(filter(
    lambda item: item[1]['grade'] >= 85 and item[1]['attendance'] >= 0.90,
    students.items()
))
```

### Transformation with Lambda

```python
# Transform dictionary values
temperatures_f = {'NYC': 68, 'LA': 75, 'Chicago': 45, 'Miami': 82}

# Convert Fahrenheit to Celsius
temperatures_c = dict(map(lambda item: (item[0], (item[1] - 32) * 5/9),
                         temperatures_f.items()))

# Using lambda with dictionary comprehension
temperatures_c_comp = {city: (temp - 32) * 5/9 for city, temp in temperatures_f.items()}

# Transform with reduce
from functools import reduce

# Find student with highest grade using reduce
students_scores = {'Alice': 95, 'Bob': 87, 'Charlie': 92, 'Diana': 98}
top_student = reduce(lambda a, b: a if students_scores[a] > students_scores[b] else b,
                    students_scores.keys())
```

sections.title: 8. Advanced Dictionary Operations {#advanced-operations}
sections.body:
### defaultdict and Counter

```python
from collections import defaultdict, Counter

# defaultdict for automatic default values
dd = defaultdict(list)
words = ['apple', 'banana', 'apple', 'cherry', 'banana', 'apple']

for word in words:
    dd[word[0]].append(word)  # Group by first letter

print(dict(dd))  # {'a': ['apple', 'apple', 'apple'], 'b': ['banana', 'banana'], 'c': ['cherry']}

# Counter for counting
word_count = Counter(words)
print(word_count)  # Counter({'apple': 3, 'banana': 2, 'cherry': 1})
print(word_count.most_common(2))  # [('apple', 3), ('banana', 2)]

# defaultdict with lambda
dd_with_lambda = defaultdict(lambda: 'Unknown')
dd_with_lambda['known'] = 'Known value'
print(dd_with_lambda['unknown'])  # 'Unknown'
```

### OrderedDict and ChainMap

```python
from collections import OrderedDict, ChainMap

# OrderedDict (less needed in Python 3.7+)
ordered = OrderedDict()
ordered['first'] = 1
ordered['second'] = 2
ordered['third'] = 3

# ChainMap for multiple dictionaries
defaults = {'color': 'red', 'user': 'guest'}
environment = {'user': 'admin'}
command_line = {'color': 'blue'}

config = ChainMap(command_line, environment, defaults)
print(config['color'])  # 'blue' (from command_line)
print(config['user'])   # 'admin' (from environment)
print(dict(config))     # Combined view
```

### Dictionary Merging (Python 3.9+)

```python
# Union operators (Python 3.9+)
dict1 = {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
dict2 = {'c': 3, 'd': 4}
dict3 = {'b': 5, 'e': 6}

# Merge dictionaries
merged = dict1 | dict2  # {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3, 'd': 4}
updated = dict1 | dict3  # {'a': 1, 'b': 5, 'e': 6} - dict3 values override

# In-place merge
dict1 |= dict2  # Modifies dict1

# Alternative methods for older Python versions
merged_old = {**dict1, **dict2}  # Unpacking
dict1.update(dict2)  # In-place update
```

### Dictionary Unpacking and Keyword Arguments

```python
def create_user(name, age, city, **kwargs):
    user = {'name': name, 'age': age, 'city': city}
    user.update(kwargs)
    return user

# Unpacking dictionary as arguments
user_data = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 30, 'city': 'Boston'}
additional_data = {'profession': 'Engineer', 'salary': 75000}

user = create_user(**user_data, **additional_data)
print(user)  # Complete user dictionary
```

sections.title: 9. Performance and Memory {#performance}
sections.body:
### Performance Considerations

```python
import time
from collections import defaultdict

# Efficient grouping with defaultdict
def group_by_first_letter_efficient(words):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for word in words:
        groups[word[0]].append(word)
    return dict(groups)

# Less efficient grouping with regular dict
def group_by_first_letter_basic(words):
    groups = {}
    for word in words:
        if word[0] in groups:
            groups[word[0]].append(word)
        else:
            groups[word[0]] = [word]
    return groups

# Memory-efficient iteration
large_dict = {i: i**2 for i in range(1000000)}

# Good - iterate over items directly
for key, value in large_dict.items():
    if value > 500000:
        break

# Avoid - creates intermediate lists
# for key in list(large_dict.keys()):  # Memory intensive!
```

### Dictionary vs List Performance

```python
# Dictionary lookup: O(1) average case
user_dict = {f'user_{i}': i for i in range(10000)}

# List search: O(n) worst case
user_list = [(f'user_{i}', i) for i in range(10000)]

# Dictionary lookup is much faster for key-based access
import time

start = time.time()
result = user_dict.get('user_5000')
dict_time = time.time() - start

start = time.time()
result = next((value for key, value in user_list if key == 'user_5000'), None)
list_time = time.time() - start

print(f"Dict lookup: {dict_time:.6f}s")
print(f"List search: {list_time:.6f}s")
```
